## Overview

The Igbo (*Ndị Igbo*, formerly anglicised "Ibo") are a people of the forested southeast of Nigeria, occupying the lower Niger basin between the Niger River and the Cross River, and extending from the Nsukka escarpment in the north to the mangrove edge of the Niger Delta in the south. Their language, Igbo, belongs to the Igboid branch of the Volta–Niger subfamily of the Niger–Congo phylum, and is spoken across a dense mosaic of dialect clusters — Onitsha, Owerri, Nsukka, Awka, Ohuhu, Ika, Ikwerre and others — that historically underlay a fragmentary political landscape of autonomous village-groups rather than centralised kingdoms, with the notable exception of the ritual polity of Nri and the delta trading city-states. Total population is commonly estimated at 40–45 million in Nigeria itself, with substantial diaspora communities in the United States, the United Kingdom, and across West and Central Africa, and a much older Atlantic diaspora, since Igbo speakers formed one of the largest single components of Africans trafficked to the Americas — particularly to Virginia, Jamaica and Haiti — during the eighteenth century. In folk-culture terms the Igbo matter as the makers of the earliest known lost-wax bronzes of West Africa, unearthed at *Igbo-Ukwu* and dated to the ninth or tenth century; as the source of the *uli* body- and wall-painting tradition; of the elaborate *mmwo* and *agbogho mmuo* masquerade complexes; of the *nsibidi* ideographic script shared with neighbouring Ekoi and Efik peoples; and of the finely warp-patterned *akwete* cloth of coastal Igboland.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Akwete** — a heavy warp-faced supplementary-weft cloth woven by women on a vertical single-heddle loom in the town of Akwete in present-day Abia State, using cotton and, historically, raffia and imported silk. The characteristic wide panels carry geometric motifs — tortoise (*mbe*), python (*eke*), stools, combs — named after the households or weavers who introduced them, and are wrapped as women's two-piece attire.

**Akwa ocha** — literally "white cloth", a plain or narrow-striped hand-woven cotton associated especially with the western Igbo communities of the Anioma area, worn as a ceremonial wrapper by titled men and used for burials of elders.

***Uli*** — the indigenous painting tradition, applied in dark blue-black or reddish vegetable dye (from the *uli* berry) as curvilinear line-work on women's bodies for feasts and on the mud walls of compounds and shrine interiors. The vocabulary is a repertoire of stylised, asymmetric motifs — moon and star discs, python coils, yam tendrils, python jaws, *nzu* dots, combs, feathers — arranged in open compositions that were canonised into modern easel painting by the Nsukka school of Uche Okeke and Obiora Udechukwu.

***Nsibidi*** — an ideographic sign system shared with the neighbouring Ekoi (Ejagham), Efik and Ibibio, historically transmitted through the *Ekpe* / *Mgbe* leopard society. Signs — for love, journey, dispute, marriage, death — appear incised on calabashes and pottery, painted on skin and cloth, and drawn on the ground; the same signs travelled across the Atlantic and are ancestral to the *anaforuana* graphic tradition of Afro-Cuban Abakuá.

**Motif vocabulary.** *Mbe* (tortoise, cunning), *eke* (python, ancestral, guardian of Idemili), *ọka* (comb), *ọnwa* (moon disc), *kpakpando* (star), *ji* (yam, male wealth), *odu* (elephant tusk), *ọfọ* (staff of authority), *agwu* (spiral, divination), and the interlaced *nsibidi* signs incorporated into wall painting and textile.

### Clothing & dress

Everyday historical dress was minimal in the humid forest zone: for men a wrapper (*akwa mgbochi*) knotted at the waist, often of *akwa ocha* or imported Manchester "George" cloth, with the torso bare or covered by a loose shirt (*isiagu* — a red or black velvet tunic printed with the head of a lion, associated with title-holders); for women a two-piece wrapper covering waist to ankle with a matching upper cloth (*ichafu* head-tie), the young unmarried body decorated with *uli* and with strings of waist beads (*jigida*). Titled men (*ozo*, *nze*) wear a red cap (*okpu agu* or *okpu ododo*), sometimes trimmed with an eagle feather, and carry an ivory or wooden staff (*ọfọ*) and a horse-tail flywhisk. Titled women (*lolo*, *omu*) wear elephant-tusk ivory anklets (*odu*) and coral bead necklaces. In coastal and delta communities the influence of the Efik and Ijaw fed elaborate coral and George-cloth wedding ensembles; among the maiden dancers of the *agbogho mmuo* masquerade, the human body itself is masked and re-covered in a tight patterned cloth suit painted with *uli*-derived designs. Today the *isiagu* over a wrapper, with red cap, has become a pan-Igbo formal costume for men.

### Architecture

Traditional Igbo architecture is a courtyard compound (*ezi na ụlọ*) enclosed by a mud wall and a woven-mat or carved wooden gate, containing a central open yard, the household head's reception hut (*obi* or *obu*), separate sleeping houses for each wife, granaries, and a kitchen. Walls are of puddled red laterite (*aja*) built in coursed layers, roofed originally with thatched raffia palm and, from the twentieth century, with corrugated iron. The *obi* is a rectangular open-fronted pavilion whose façade columns and mud walls carry low-relief modelled and painted decoration — geometric bands, *uli* motifs, animal figures — and inside which the *ọfọ* staff and family shrines are kept. The most elaborate architectural form is the ***mbari*** house of the Owerri and Okigwe area: a large earthen shrine-pavilion commissioned by a community for the earth goddess *Ala* (or another deity), built in secrecy by an initiated team over months or years, and filled with painted, life-size unfired clay figures of the deity, her retinue, humans, animals, colonial officers, cars and aeroplanes — a deliberately encyclopaedic tableau. Once completed and unveiled, the *mbari* is left to weather back into the earth. Village architecture also includes the ceremonial meeting-house or *ilo* square with its shade tree, and the shrine forest (*ọfịa mmụọ*), left uncleared as habitation of ancestors and spirits.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Igbo pottery is women's work in most communities, hand-built by coil-and-pinch without the wheel and open-fired; the town of **Ishiagu** (Ebonyi) and the villages around **Inyi** and **Afikpo** are among the surviving centres, producing water pots (*ite*), cooking pots, ritual bowls, and the tall, elegantly waisted *udu* — a globular pot with a second lateral opening that also functions as a bass percussion instrument. Ritual pots for *Ala* shrines and for the yam cult are modelled with faces, snakes and figural attachments. Metalwork of the highest order is represented by the ninth–tenth-century lost-wax bronzes of ***Igbo-Ukwu***, excavated by Thurstan Shaw — regalia, staff heads, pendants and the celebrated openwork *roped pot* — showing a mastery of casting comparable to any in the medieval world and predating the classical bronzes of Ife and Benin by centuries. The historical smithing town of **Awka** supplied ironwork, ceremonial swords (*mma*), hoes and the incised *ọfọ*-related staffs across Igboland, its blacksmiths travelling seasonally as a specialised guild. Household objects include the carved wooden ***okwa*** — round or rectangular bowls with lids, used for kola nuts, offerings and yam presentation — mortars and pestles, low three- or four-legged stools carved from a single block, and the *ikoro* slit-log community drum. The ***ikenga***, a horned wooden figure representing a man's right hand, strength and personal accomplishment, is carved for adult men and kept on a personal shrine; on the owner's death it is broken. The ***ọfọ*** — a short, naturally jointed stick from the *ọfọ* tree (*Detarium*) — is the emblem of truth and lineage authority held by elders and *ozo* title-holders.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The most conspicuous Igbo body ornament is coral: heavy strands of red coral beads (*mgbaji* and larger neck pieces) worn by titled women, brides and chiefs, historically obtained through the Atlantic and trans-Saharan trade and cascaded down the chest and around the ankles for weddings. Ivory anklets and armlets (*odu*) — some large and heavy enough to require support while walking — signalled the highest female titles, especially in the Onitsha and Nri areas. Younger women wear multi-strand waist beads (*jigida*) under the wrapper, tinkling as they move. Brass anklets and leg-rings, worked by Awka smiths, and cowrie ornaments were common in the interior. Facial and body scarification (*ichi*) — a set of parallel vertical or radiating incisions on the forehead and temples — historically marked initiation into the *nze na ozo* title system, particularly in the Nri–Awka heartland, and appears already on the Igbo-Ukwu bronze heads. *Uli* body-painting, applied by women to women and to brides using a thin stick or feather, complemented the more permanent *ichi*. Kaolin chalk (*nzu*) is dabbed around the eyes and along the arms as a marker of ritual purity, welcome, and communication with the ancestors.

## Music & performance

Igbo musical life is built around the drum ensemble and the call-and-response chorus. The signature instruments are the ***ikoro*** — a large slit log drum kept in the village square and struck to convene assemblies, warn of danger, or announce a death — the *ekwe* (smaller slit gong), the *udu* clay pot drum played by striking the side opening with the palm to produce a deep bass note, the *ogene* iron double bell whose ostinato underpins most dance music, the hourglass tension drum (*ịgba* or *kalangu*), the flute (*ọjà*), the thumb piano (*ubọ aka*), and the pluriarc *ubọ* lute of the western Igbo. Vocal genres include the topical praise and satire singing of *egwu ekpili* accompanied by *ubọ aka* and *ogene*, the massed women's work songs of yam-planting and pounding, war-dance songs (*egwu ọta*), and the highlife-derived Igbo popular music that flowered around Onitsha from the 1950s in the hands of Osita Osadebe, Celestine Ukwu and Oliver De Coque. Praise-singers (*egwu ọma*) improvise proverb-laden verse over the ensemble, and the *ọjà* flute is used by dance leaders to call named steps and to salute individual dancers by their praise-name.

## Dance & theatre

Igbo dance is inseparable from masquerade (***mmanwụ*** or ***mmwo***), regarded as the visible manifestation of ancestral spirits (*ndị ichie*) rather than as theatre in the European sense. Masquerades are the property of men's secret societies, into which boys are initiated; women and non-initiates observe from a formal distance. The repertoire ranges across registers: the tall, stately ***ijele***, a house-sized composite mask of the northern Igbo inscribed by UNESCO in 2009 on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity as the "Ijele Masquerade", carried by a single dancer beneath a tiered structure hung with mirrors, cloth panels and figurines of everyday life; the beautiful, white-faced ***agbogho mmụọ*** ("maiden spirit") masks of the Onitsha and Nri area, worn by young men dancing in mincing imitation of idealised girlhood; the aggressive, dark, horned *ọgbagba* and *ịzaga* warrior and stilt masks; and the satirical, grotesque *mgbedike* ("time of the brave") masks used to police behaviour and lampoon offenders. Masquerade outings mark the second burial of elders, the New Yam festival, and calendar rites. The ***ekpe*** / ***mgbe*** leopard society, shared with the Cross River peoples, also stages masked dances tied to the *nsibidi* sign system. Alongside masquerade, competitive men's *atilogwu* acrobatic dance and women's *nkwa umuagbogho* maiden dances survive as staged forms.

## Festivals & rituals

The pivotal calendar rite is the ***Iwa Ji*** or ***Iri Ji*** ("new yam eating") festival, held in most communities between August and October at the harvest of the new yam crop, at which the eldest man or title-holder offers the first yams to *Ala* (the earth goddess) and to the ancestors before the community may eat them; the festival is accompanied by masquerade, wrestling (*mgba*), and the exchange of kola nut. ***Ọfala*** is the annual outing of a traditional ruler (*Obi* or *Igwe*), particularly celebrated at Onitsha, when the monarch emerges in full regalia to dance before his people. Life-cycle rites include the presentation of the newborn to the earth on the fourth market day (the Igbo week is a four-day cycle: *Eke*, *Orie*, *Afọ*, *Nkwọ*), circumcision, the *iru mgbede* seclusion of a bride, the elaborate *igba nkwụ* wine-carrying wedding at which the bride identifies her groom by presenting him with a cup of palm wine, and the two-stage burial of elders in which the "second burial" months or years after death releases the deceased into the ranks of the ancestors. Divination is performed by *dibịa* priests using the *afa* system of cast seeds and cowries, and the breaking and sharing of kola nut (*ọjị*) — with its formal prayer *onye wetara ọjị wetara ndụ*, "he who brings kola brings life" — opens every significant meeting.

## Foodways

The staple around which Igbo cuisine is organised is the yam (*ji*), a crop so central that its cultivation is ritualised, its planting reserved to men, and its abundance the measure of a household's standing; boiled yam with palm oil and pepper (*ji mmanụ*) is the archetypal morning meal, and pounded yam (*utara ji* or, in Nigerian English, "pounded yam") accompanies the great soups. Cassava, cocoyam, plantain and rice have joined the staple set. The characteristic soups (*ofe*) are thick, palm-oil based, and served with a starchy swallow: ***ofe onugbu*** (bitter-leaf soup, thickened with cocoyam paste), ***ofe egusi*** (ground melon-seed soup), ***ofe ọha*** (with *ọha* leaves and cocoyam), ***ofe nsala*** ("white soup", palm-oil-free, thickened with yam and flavoured with *utazi* and *uziza*), and ***ofe akwụ*** (palm-fruit concentrate). ***Abacha*** — shredded cassava dressed with palm oil, potash, *utazi* leaves, garden egg and dried fish — is the signature salad of the western Igbo. ***Ugba*** (fermented oil-bean seed) and ***ọkpa*** (steamed Bambara-nut pudding of the Nsukka area) are ceremonial and market foods. Palm wine (*mmanya ngwọ* and the stronger *mmanya nkwụ*) tapped fresh from the palm at dawn is the ritual drink offered to guests and required for weddings; kola nut and *alligator pepper* precede it in every formal greeting.

## Oral tradition & literature

Igbo oral literature is proverb-saturated — the saying *ilu bụ mmanụ e ji eri okwu*, "proverbs are the palm oil with which words are eaten", is itself proverbial — and structured around the folktale (*ifo* or *akụkọ ifo*), the historical legend (*akụkọ ala*), the riddle (*agwụgwa*), the incantation, and the praise-name (*aha ọma*) that condenses a person's or lineage's history into a single epithet. Tortoise (*mbe* or *mbekwu*) is the trickster hero of the folktale cycle, matching wits with elephant, lion and the sky-god. The *dibịa afa* diviner works a corpus of chanted verses that name the ancestors and describe the case at hand. In modern letters the Igbo tradition produced Chinua Achebe, whose *Things Fall Apart* (1958) translates the proverbial texture and the ritual world of a late-nineteenth-century Igbo village into English prose and remains the single most widely read African novel; Flora Nwapa, Cyprian Ekwensi, Buchi Emecheta, Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie and Chigozie Obioma have continued the line. Written Igbo literature in the Onwu orthography — poetry, novels and drama — has a smaller but continuous presence since the mid-twentieth century.

## Language & religion

Igbo is a tonal language with a high–low–downstep system, written since the 1960s in the standard Onwu Latin orthography; the recognised standard literary form is a compromise dialect drawing on Owerri and Umuahia, though dialectal variation across Igboland is extensive enough that speakers of the peripheral western (Ika, Ukwuani) and northern (Nsukka) varieties often converse more comfortably in Nigerian English or Pidgin. The traditional religion (*Ọdịnala*) is centred on a distant creator god (*Chukwu* or *Chineke*), a pantheon of *alusi* — including *Ala* (the earth), *Amadioha* (thunder), *Idemili* (river and python), *Agwu* (divination), *Ikenga* (personal drive) — the ancestors (*ndị ichie*), and the personal spirit (*chi*) attached to each individual at birth. Ritual authority is distributed rather than centralised, held by titled elders of the *nze na ozo* system, by *dibịa* priest-diviners, and, in the historical Nri polity, by the *Eze Nri*, a ritual king whose sanction validated the taking of titles across Igboland. Christianity — brought by Anglican CMS and Roman Catholic missions from the mid-nineteenth century, and today reinforced by an exuberant Pentecostal sector — is the majority religion, with the *Ọdịnala* substrate persisting in life-cycle ritual, kola-nut etiquette, and syncretic prophetic movements such as the Aladura churches on the Yoruba–Igbo interface.
